front.title: Deep32: Measured Retrieval, Research Behaviour and Answer Quality in Release 0.1.0-alpha.3

abstract.t: D32-TR-1 described how Deep32 is built. This report measures it. It covers release 0.1.0-alpha.3 and brings together three kinds of evidence: the retrieval evaluation on 696 labelled questions, the recorded telemetry of four research answers produced through the Ask window, and a blind comparison of Deep32 with three general assistants on three hard routing benchmarks.

In the blind comparison all four systems derived the core results correctly. Deep32, answering from its local corpus with web search disabled and with gpt-6.2-sol as its headend model, scored 268.5 of 300 under the headline rater against 270 for Claude with web research, and its answers carried the most checkable evidence (69 of 75); Gemini and ChatGPT scored 226 and 211.5. A second blind rater agreed within 2.3 points per answer, and an earlier grading with the names visible is listed beside them. Deep32 is the only system that every grader placed first or second. The comparison is small and its limits are stated with it.

Every number in this report is labelled by where it comes from: the source code, a log or build record, a calculation on recorded values, or the author's judgement. Where the record is missing, the report says so. The limits of the evidence, and the evaluation still to be run before a beta, are stated in full.

note.name: Status of This Document
note.t: This is Deep32 Technical Report 2 (D32-TR-2), the measurement report for Deep32 release 0.1.0-alpha.3, published by its author. It is not a product of the IETF or of any other standards body and has no standing there. It uses the RFC format to match D32-TR-1 .
Errors can be reported on the project's issue tracker. This version has not yet been deposited with a DOI.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Deep32 lets an agentic language model answer networking questions from a local corpus of RFCs and vendor documentation, and check its quotations against the stored text . The design report explains how. Three questions remained open after it:

ul.li: How well does the retrieval pipeline put the right passage in front of the model?
What does the model actually do with eleven tools when it researches a hard question?
Are the answers better than those of capable assistants that search the open web?

section.t: This report answers the first two with recorded measurements, and the third with a blind comparison that is small and is described with its limits. Release 0.1.0-alpha.3 is the system measured.

section.name: How Evidence Is Labelled
section.t: Each statement of fact carries one of four labels:

dl.dd: Read from the source code or the shipped configuration of the release.
A value written by the system itself: a log, a build report, a database count.
Arithmetic on recorded values; the method is given.
The author's assessment, including the grading in .
One question asked through the Ask window and answered, from submission to the end of the answer.
One call from the headend to the hosted model. A run makes many.
One call of one of the eleven Deep32 tools, such as get_section or verify_quote.
The tokens the headend sends with one model request: instructions, tool definitions, the question and everything researched so far in the run.
The program that runs the model for Ask: here, a relay on the user's PC that starts the Codex app-server for each turn.

section.name: System Under Test
section.t: The measured deployment is release 0.1.0-alpha.3 at update sequence 4, on the three machines D32-TR-1 describes: the Workstation (OpenBSD), which holds the corpus, the indexes, the engine, the gateway and the Ask window; the Forge, a GPU host that computes query embeddings and reranker scores; and the headend PC, which runs the relay. [Code]
Every tool call goes from the model, through the relay and the pinned D32U/1 link, back to the Workstation's own gateway and engine. The PC holds no index. [Code]
Changes since D32-TR-1 that bear on the measurements:

ul.li: The top eight hits of a search now carry up to 3,200 characters of text instead of 2,400. [Code]
The default answer depth caps its search rounds by search size: Full 4, Half 5, Light 6, plus one batch of quotation checks. D32-TR-1 described at most three rounds. [Code]
The engine serves one search at a time with a queue of 16, behind a first-in, first-out gate for the reranker. [Code]
Quotations with omissions are checked part by part within one section, each part at most 300 characters after the previous one. [Code]

The Ask headend runs a fresh, isolated Codex app-server process for every turn, read-only, with shell, web search and automatic delegation to other agents disabled. Before it serves any tool call it checks the process's configuration, its feature flags, its tool list (exactly eleven tools) and its model list. [Code]

section.t: The hosted model in every measured run was gpt-6.2-sol. One run used the reasoning effort "max" and three used "ultra". Because the headend disables delegation, "ultra" runs at the same reasoning depth as "max" in this setting. [Code] [Record]

section.name: Corpus
section.t: The public knowledge-base generation of this release, d32kb-20261115cr, holds the collections in . [Record]

The chunks hold about 24.9 million lexical tokens (a regular-expression count, not a model tokenizer count) in 156,294 sections. Side tables add the metadata of 9,858 RFCs, of which 9,493 are metadata only; 1,235 errata over 282 RFCs; 2,374 IANA registry rows; and a command-line index of 150,917 rows. [Record]

The Cisco documents are 263 TechNotes, 126 configuration guides, 48 command references and 52 other documents. 91 carry an IOS XE 17.x release, 11 a 26.x release, and 320 carry no release at all, 237 of them TechNotes. There are no exact duplicate documents; 4,361 chunks share their text with another and are folded into one hit at query time. [Record]

A deployment can add its own local collections. The measured deployment had some; they are outside this report, and the four measured answers cite only documents from the public collections above. [Record]

section.name: Retrieval Quality
section.t: The retrieval evaluation of D32-TR-1 is restated here because it remains the strongest measurement of the system. 696 answerable questions, each with its relevant passages labelled in the source text, were run through the gateway on 2 November 2026, against the release 0.1.0-alpha.2 design and an earlier corpus generation; it was not repeated on the deployment measured in , which differs in the width of the top hits, in serving one search at a time, and in searching vectors exactly rather than through an approximate index. Searches fuse a BM25 and a dense ranking by reciprocal rank fusion and rerank the first 15 candidates with a cross-encoder. A question is a hit at rank k when a labelled passage is among the first k results. [Record]

Paired over the 696 questions, reranking won 102 questions and lost 9 at rank 1, and won 6 and lost none in the top eight. The mean reciprocal rank at 10 rose from 0.882 to 0.970. Of the 31 questions still missed at rank 1, 7 had an answering passage that carried no label, 21 were reranker misorderings, and 3 left the relevant passage outside the reranker's first 15 candidates. [Record]

Three limits apply. The questions were written with a language model and labelled from pooled results; two small blind audits agreed with the labels on 22 of 27 and 15 of 16 items; and the 30 out-of-scope questions of the set have no reported result. Retrieval quality is also not answer quality: a hit puts the right passage in front of the model, and the answer can still misuse it. [Record]

section.name: How an Answer Is Researched
section.t: Four runs were recorded on 23 November 2026: an introductory OSPF question ("Explain OSPF from the ground up ...", with the modifiers d, v, o and g) and Benchmarks 001 to 003 of . The benchmark answers were kept by hand; their link to the logged runs rests on run order and the author's record. The relay and the Codex app-server logged every tool call, every turn's token use and, for the last run in full, the context of every model request. [Record]

section.name: Time
section.t: Research is the time from the first to the last tool call; writing is the time from the last tool call to the end of the answer, and includes the model's last reasoning. The tools themselves account for little of the research time: a section read took a median of 72 to 98 ms and a search 2.3 to 4.3 s, and in Benchmark 003 all code cells together took 26.3 s of its 282 s of research. Most of the time is the model thinking between calls. [Record] [Calc]

section.name: What the Model Did
section.t: Reading whole sections dominates: 229 of the 448 calls, 51 %. The model searches a few times, then reads the sections the searches point to, checks every command it will print against the command index at the pinned release, and checks its quotations. Every call returned HTTP 200 and the relay refused none. Four calls returned a tool-level error (two malformed quotation batches, one unknown section, one RFC not in the corpus), and in each case the model corrected its next call. [Record]

section.name: Tokens and Context
section.t: Input reaches millions of tokens because every model request sends the whole context again: about 100,000 tokens of instructions, tool definitions and question, plus everything researched so far. Benchmark 003, the one run whose log kept every request, shows it directly: its 33 recorded contexts grew from 102,749 to 241,629 tokens and sum to 5,923,371, which is 98.1 % of its recorded input. Almost all of that input is read from the provider's prompt cache, because each request begins with the previous request's context. [Record] [Calc]

Benchmark 003 used less than half the input of Benchmark 001 although it made more tool calls (113 against 81). It sent 3.3 tool calls per model request (3.4 per code cell), in parallel, where the other runs sent about one, so it needed 34 requests where they needed 86 to 137. The number of requests, more than the work done, decides the input. [Record] [Calc]

section.name: Answer Quality: A Blind Comparison
section.t: Three benchmarks, written by the author, test whether an answer can derive results from protocol rules rather than recall them. Deep32 and three general assistants each answered all three once, and every answer was graded blind, by two raters, against an answer key solved first from the question and the standards. [Judgement]

dl.dd: OSPFv2 external route selection: five Type 5 LSAs for one prefix at an ABR, with forwarding addresses, ASBR entries in two areas and both settings of RFC1583Compatibility. Eight questions: eligibility, the selected route under each setting, three variants, ECMP, the order of evaluation and verification commands by layer .

BGP route-reflection oscillation: two route reflectors, three exits in two neighbouring ASes, MED and IGP cost. Nine question groups: proof that no stable state exists, the IGP-cost threshold at which one appears, always-compare-med, four ADD-PATH cases, forwarding deflection, identical cluster IDs and configuration .

An MPLS L3VPN escalation: overlapping routes in two VRFs, an OSPF sham link and backdoor, PE-CE domain IDs and the DN bit, label traces through a failure and a micro-loop, a routing feedback loop, and ten conflicting operator reports to reconcile .

section.name: Systems and Conditions

tr.td: gpt-6.2-sol, effort ultra, modifiers d, v, o and g (recorded)
Local corpus only; web search disabled
GPT-6 Pro, maximum, Deep Research (as selected)
Gemini 4 Neon, High, Deep Research (as selected)

section.t: Only Deep32's settings are recorded by the system. The settings of the other three are those I selected in each application; the answers show web use (links to RFC Editor, Cisco and community pages) but carry no record of model or date. The conditions are not matched: the general assistants could search the whole web, and Deep32's question carried four modifier sentences asking for deep research, a long answer, verification steps and troubleshooting. The comparison is between systems as an engineer would use them, not between models.

The answers were captured as text: copied from Deep32, Claude and ChatGPT, and converted from Gemini's PDF exports. Two capture effects matter. ChatGPT's citations, links in its own interface, survive in the copy only as opaque markers; and the PDF conversion fused some of Gemini's footnote numbers into values and broke some tables.

section.name: Grading

ol.li: Masking. Each benchmark's four answers were given the letters A to D in a different order, system names were replaced, and the Deep32 question line was removed. The key to the letters was held apart from the raters.
Key first. The first rater solved each benchmark from its question alone, with the derivation, the governing rule and its source line for each item, before opening any answer.

Sources. Facts could come only from the question, the RFC and Cisco texts of the corpus (read as plain files, not through Deep32), and arithmetic. No web and no facts from memory: vendor behaviour that those texts do not document was marked unverifiable and neither rewarded nor penalised.

Scoring. Correctness 40 (agreement with the key), evidence 25 (primary, specific citations that say what the answer claims, spot-checked against the texts), completeness 15, caution 10 (assumptions, release qualification, labelled inference) and clarity 10.
Re-check. The first rater then tried to refute its own key on every point where the answers differed. No key item changed.

Second rater. A second rater, a different model, scored the same masked answers on the same rubric against the same key, without seeing the first scores, and was asked to show any key item wrong from the RFC text. It upheld every item.

section.t: The first rater was Claude Opus 5.5 and the second Claude Mythos 5.2, each run as a separate instance per benchmark, working from files. I take the second rater's scores as the headline: it is the stronger model, and it scored against a key that had by then been solved, re-checked and upheld. The first rater's scores are given beside them.

A third set of scores predates this grading. ChatGPT (GPT-6) scored the same twelve answers with the system names visible, by its own criteria and without the key. Those scores are listed in for comparison. They are not blind and carry no weight in the conclusions.

section.name: Results

table.name: Blind Scores from the Headline Rater (out of 100 per Benchmark)

figure.name: Total Blind Score over Three Benchmarks, Headline Rater

table.name: Score by Part from the Headline Rater, Summed over the Three Benchmarks

section.t: Under the headline rater Deep32 placed second on Benchmark 001 by one point, first on 002 by 1.5 and second on 003 by two. In total it is 1.5 points behind Claude and more than 40 ahead of the other two, and it has the highest evidence score. [Judgement]

table.name: Scores by Benchmark from the Other Two Graders

section.t: "Named" in means that the grader saw the system names. The first rater's evidence scores, out of 75, were Deep32 71, Claude 61, Gemini 41 and ChatGPT 31.

The two blind raters agree closely. Over the twelve answers they differ by 2.3 points on average and by 8.5 at most (ChatGPT on 002, where the headline rater gave less for citations that cannot be resolved). Both put Claude and Deep32 first and second on every benchmark, in an order that differs between them on 001 and 002, and both give Deep32 the highest evidence score, 69 and 71 of 75. [Calc]

The unblinded grader differs from the blind raters by 15 and 13.5 points per answer on average. It placed all four systems within eight points of each other, with Deep32 first and Gemini second. Deep32 is the only system that every grader placed first or second. [Calc]

section.name: What Decided the Scores
section.t: All four systems got every core computed result right in all three benchmarks: the eligible LSAs and selected routes of 001, the absence of a stable state and the threshold of 002, the cost ranges, the TTL trace of the micro-loop and the minimum set of false reports of 003. None fell into the planted traps, such as using the reflector's router ID in the tie-break of 002. Correctness spans 12 points of 120 under the headline rater and nine under the first. The scores were decided by evidence, by errors outside the core results, and by completeness. [Judgement]

Evidence. Every citation the two raters checked in a Deep32 answer matched the corpus text at the cited document and lines; a few pointed at passages that fit the claim only loosely. Claude quoted RFC and Cisco text exactly by section, without line numbers, and every checkable quotation matched; some rested on documents outside the corpus, such as RFC 3345. Gemini mixed primary sources with forums, blogs and links its export left as "unknown_url". ChatGPT's citations could not be resolved from the text. [Judgement]
Errors outside the core results, by system:

ul.li: Gemini: that disabling RFC1583Compatibility also changes the summary-cost calculation (001); "MUST NOT" for the "should not assume" of RFC 7911 (002); that RFC 4577 copies the MED into the Type 3 metric (003); and a Cisco command's effect on DN-bit checks stated from another platform's note (003).
ChatGPT: an ECMP rationale built on a wrong premise about the associated area of external paths (001); a cycle summary that skips a state (002); a wrong section number (003).
Claude: none affecting a result. It was the only system to point out that Benchmark 003 contains an equal-cost tie that contradicts its own "no ECMP" premise.

Deep32: none affecting a result. It lost points for configuration given as templates, a thin treatment of the operational effects in 002, and leftovers of its working process in the answer text ("Full search, deep mode.", "I'll verify ...").

section.t: Leaving clarity out of the headline totals puts Deep32 ahead of Claude, 247 to 243. Leaving evidence out puts Claude ahead, 214 to 199.5. Deep32's place at the top rests on its evidence, and its shortfall against Claude is in detail of correctness, completeness and clarity. [Calc]

section.name: The Headend Model
section.t: Deep32 does not write its answers; its headend model does. In these runs the headend was gpt-6.2-sol at effort ultra, so the Deep32 scores are those of that model working through Deep32's tools and corpus. Another headend would give other answers and other scores. [Record]

ChatGPT, a model of the same vendor researching on the open web, scored 57 points lower than Deep32 under the headline rater (211.5 against 268.5) and 52 lower under the first rater. Most of the difference is evidence, 25 against 69, and part of that is the capture effect described in . The two are different models with different instructions, so the gap is not a controlled measure of what the corpus and the tools add. The matched-model arms planned in are designed to measure that. [Calc] [Judgement]

ul.li: Both blind raters are Claude models, and one of the systems compared is Claude. Names were masked, but style can identify a model. Deep32's headend model, gpt-6.2-sol, is not from Anthropic.

Each family of grader placed first a system whose answers a model of its own vendor wrote: the Claude raters placed Claude first, and the GPT grader placed Deep32 first. Only the blind raters scored against a key.
Masking was weaker for Deep32 than for the others: its answers end with the list of sections read and cite corpus documents by key, which a rater can recognise.

Evidence was checked against the RFC and Cisco texts that Deep32 indexes. Answers that cite those texts by line are easier to confirm, and web sources outside them could only be marked unverifiable. This favours Deep32's evidence score, although an unverifiable source was not counted against an answer.
Capture lowered ChatGPT's evidence and Gemini's clarity scores (). Their totals should be read with that in mind; their correctness and caution scores are not affected.

Two blind raters, one answer per system, three benchmarks. The second rater scored against the first rater's key, so the two are independent in scoring and not in the key. The difference between the top two is smaller than the difference between the raters.
Deep32's result is that of one headend model at one effort setting ().

section.name: One Answer in Detail
section.t: The introductory OSPF answer (the first run) is the one whose full text and full telemetry are both on record. It cites 17 source documents, all primary: four RFCs (2328 , 3101, 5340, 5838), six Cisco configuration guides and command references pinned to the Catalyst 9300 17.9 release, and seven Cisco TechNotes. It carries about 107 citations to a document and line range, and 18 quotations: 14 marked exact and 4 marked normalized, against 18 accepted quotation-check calls. Its last lines list every section it read. [Record]

It also found a contradiction in Cisco's own guide: one passage gives the OSPF reference bandwidth as "10" and another as 100 Mbps. The answer quoted both, preferred the default table and the command reference, and told the reader how to check a live device. [Record]

section.name: What "Verified" Means
section.t: verify_quote looks for the quotation in the stored source text of the cited document: first verbatim and case-sensitive, inside the cited section and then anywhere in the document; failing that, after mapping typographic quotes and dashes and removing whitespace and hyphen runs. It returns where it matched, by section and source line. [Code]

A label of exact or normalized therefore proves that the words exist in the source, and where. It does not prove that the passage supports the sentence it is attached to, and most claims in an answer are paraphrases with a citation, which no mechanism checks for support. An optional script on the relay compares an answer's quotations, RFC citations and specific values with what its tool calls returned; it was off in the measured deployment. [Code] [Record]

section.name: What the Code Enforces and What the Model Is Asked To Do
section.t: Deep32 splits its guarantees between code and instructions. The split matters for any claim about answer quality, because instructed behaviour depends on the model following it.

tr.td: Only the eleven read-only tools; no shell, web or delegation
At most 300 tool calls and 3,600 s per turn; 4 calls in flight
Hybrid search, reranking, tiers, release filters, quotation matching
Searching the corpus before answering; no answers from memory
Reading whole sections; checking every command at the pinned release
Stopping rules for rounds; counter-evidence searches; marking disputes
Checking the corpus outline before writing "not in corpus"
Question modifiers such as d, v, o and g
Instruction: each adds a fixed sentence to the question

section.t: The four recorded runs show the instructions being followed: section reads and command checks dominate the tool mix, and the one answer on record quotes only what it checked. Four runs do not show how often a model departs from them. [Record] [Judgement]

ul.li: The comparison in is three benchmarks and one answer per system, graded by two raters of one model family. It is evidence, not a ranking that would survive a larger study.
The benchmark answers of the other systems were produced in their own applications with web access; their models, settings and dates were not recorded with the same care as Deep32's.
No answer was tested on a router. Correctness was judged against an answer key derived from the questions' own data and the RFC and Cisco texts of the corpus.

The relay does not keep question texts, answer texts, tool arguments or the result of each quotation check. The three benchmark answers were kept by hand; their association with the logged runs rests on run order and the author's record.
Codex keeps only its last 1,000 log rows per thread, so the per-request record is complete for one run of four.
Release metadata is missing on 320 of 489 Cisco documents, mostly TechNotes; release pinning cannot act on them.

section.name: Evaluation Plan for the Beta
section.t: The beta release waits on a claim-level evaluation designed to remove the limits above:

ul.li: 40 to 60 held-out questions, stratified by kind (defaults and timers, command syntax at a release, RFC against Cisco behaviour, troubleshooting, design), each with a reference answer split into atomic claims and their sources.

The same model and effort in every arm: Deep32; the same model with no tools; the same model with plain dense retrieval over the same chunks; and ablations of reranking, section reads and quotation checks.

Scores for correctness, support of each claim by its cited passage, citation precision, release qualification and calibrated refusal; graded blind by two judges, with disagreements and a random fifth adjudicated by a person.
Paired analysis by question with effect sizes and bootstrap intervals; every question, answer, tool call and quotation result kept with the run.

section.t: The gates set for the beta are at most 2 % fabricated claims, every out-of-corpus probe refused, and every printed citation exact.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: The hosted model sees the question, the retrieved passages and its own reasoning; nothing else leaves the user's machines. Retrieved text can carry instructions; the tools mark it as data and the model is told to treat it so, but a passage can still steer the model within the eleven tools. The measurements in this report were taken from logs that hold no question or answer text, and local collections outside the release are not described.

section.name: Data and Provenance
section.t: The run telemetry was read from the relay's call, usage and event logs and from the Codex app-server's log database, all on the headend PC, opened read-only. The corpus figures come from the bundle metadata, the build reports and database counts of the public generation. The retrieval figures are those of D32-TR-1, Section 13. The per-run summary and the per-call timeline are published beside this report in the data folder.
